newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Chronology of PNG's struggle on Bougainville.
newsitem.headline: Chronology of PNG's struggle on Bougainville.

text.p: Following is a brief chronology of events in the Bougainville secessionist struggle against Papua New Guinea.
1988 - Land owners in Bougainville demand additional compensation from Papua New Guinea government for damage done by mining operations, begin attacking buses carrying mine workers.

May 1989 - One of the world's largest copper mines at Panguna on Bougainville suspends operations because of the unrest, depriving PNG of 40 percent of its export earnings. PNG Prime Minister Rabbie Namaliu responds with force and fighting escalates. Several hundred people killed, sparking secessionist demands from Bougainville.
May 17, 1990 - Independence declaration by self-styled Republic of Bougainville president Francis Ona. Ceasefire talks abandoned.

January, 1991 - PNG ministers and delegates from Bougainville meet in the Solomon Islands and sign the "Honiara Declaration of Peace, Reconciliation and Rehabilitation on Bougainville", but declaration breaks down when PNG forces unilaterally land in northern Bougainville, prompting fighting to start again.
1992 - Newly elected Prime Minister Paias Wingti takes a hard line, attempting to inject stability in PNG with severe internal security laws and also redoubles military efforts in Bougainville.
October 1992 - PNG troops launch a major offensive aimed at ending the secessionist crisis, but fighting bogged down and drags into 1993.
August 30, 1994 - Sir Julius Chan elected Prime Minister.
1996 - About 1,400 PNG troops attempt to encircle rebels of the Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRA) camped in the island's mountainous interior.
February, 1997 - PNG government hires foreign mercenaries to end Bougainville revolt. Australia, a major aid donor, condemns the move, as do the United States, New Zealand and others.
March 17, 1997 - PNG Defence Force Commander Brigadier General Jerry Singirok detains mercenaries and gives Chan and other ministers 48 hours to quit or be forced to do so.
